blocks.text: INTRODUCTION
The Perfumer's Work
I know you may have some questions about this course like:
“Will I be a qualified perfumer at the end of it?”
"Will I really be able to create my own fragrances and perfumes?" "Will my products really be of quality?"
The answer to all these questions is the same: "it's up to you".

If you want to enter the fragrance industry, working for large companies, and so on, you will have to take a degree in Chemistry or Cosmetic Science and also specific courses that are often sponsored or developed by fragrance houses for their internal audience.

But if you want to be an artisan perfumer or start your own business, there are other options available to you. If you're in Europe, it's a little bit more difficult to sell your own fragrances due to European Union regulations that don't apply in countries like Brazil and the US. But even then it's not impossible, it's just more work.
But back to the main point here, anyone who wants to be a perfumer should start studying and reading as much as they can and taking courses like this one.
Perfumery is not a quick thing to learn, and I will say straight away that a 1 day course will not make you a proficient perfumer, it comes with time and practice.

There is no recognized qualification for the perfumer profession such as a degree. Perfumery is both a science and an art form and it's a bit like asking if an art degree will make someone a qualified artist - that's not how it works. Yes, you will learn the techniques necessary to make a great perfume in this course, you can even take a face-to-face course with a renowned master perfumer who created a famous fragrance. But that doesn't guarantee anyone talent or creativity - it comes from within.

Perfumery is, in part, learning theory, in part, a creative spark and, above all, lots and lots of practice. All my courses here on the platform teach a lot of things, but I can't do the work for my student it must come from you!
Becoming a perfumer takes time, each and every course is just the tip of the iceberg.
The more you learn, the more you realize that you still need to learn, but luckily you don't have to do it aimlessly or alone, professionals like me are here to help you on this path.

During this course remember that making a great perfume comes with practice, so the most important advice I can give you is: pay close attention to theories and techniques, but they are nothing if you don't roll up your sleeves and start creating!
Brief History of Perfumery

A good perfume is more than an olfactory experience. It is a journey, a souvenir, an adventure, a masterpiece that mixes creativity, art and science. The truth is that perfumes are not just about scents, but about people. They can be our connection to culture, tradition, history, mythology, spirituality and, by extension, to each other. Mixing scents and creating something new requires a dash of artistry, a touch of imagination and a healthy dose of mad scientist.

The art of perfumery is over 4,000 years old, with roots in Mesopotamia, Egypt and China. Although nowadays we think of perfume as an aromatic liquid that we can apply on our skin, the word "perfume" comes from the Latin phrase "per fumare”, which means "through smoke". This primitive form of incense marks the first historical appearance of perfume. The French coined the term "parfum" that is still used throughout the world.

Perfume, then, has its origin as something deeply symbolic and often of a spiritual nature. Frankincense, myrrh and other aromatic resins, as well as herbs and woods, were often burned as part of religious settings. In fact, some cultures originally reserved the right to burn incense only for the priest and higher officials of temples. In Egypt, it was not until the Golden Age that perfume was released to the masses; before that, it was used only in rituals in honor of gods and pharaohs. The early Catholic Church had similar rules about burning certain incense sticks, considering this act a sacrament.

It didn't take long for people to realize that these fragrances also did a good job of covering up unpleasant odors, which were common since there was no culture of regular showers before. The next stage in the evolution of perfumery was to use fragrances not to cover one's scent, but to block out the scents of others. In fact, upper-class people wore specially scented gloves when going out in the city to inhale the glove's scent instead of those around them.
From this practice came the scented scarves, necklaces and medallions and, eventually, the perfume as we know it today.
The methods used to create perfume have changed dramatically over the ages.

The first perfumes were made with natural materials such as bark, wood, roots, leaves, flowers, resins and seeds. Ancient civilizations often turned fragrant materials into balms, infusing the aromatic material into oils.

Today's perfumes and fragrances are used by millions of people and are a popular fashion accessory. Both natural and synthetic ingredients are used to make perfumes that include multiple aromatic layers with different and complex notes.
Unlike its beginnings, today the perfume is accessible to the masses. It is no longer reserved for the rich and noble. Wearing perfume is now a fun way to express our personal tastes and style!

blocks.text: Artisan, Designer, Dupe and Counterfeit Perfume

The terms artisan, designer, dupe and counterfeit perfume are often confused. So since the purpose of this course is to teach you about the world of perfumery and to create your own products, it's only fair to talk about it now.

The Artisan or Niche perfume is one that is made just outside the big industries, often made by amateur perfumers like you or even by great professional perfumers. The point here is that niche perfumes are made on a smaller scale and have a great deal of originality.

When we talk about designer perfumes, we usually talk about products formulated on a large scale by large companies. They may be more expensive or cheaper, but their point is that they are always the same, always standardized. It doesn't matter if I buy this bottle in Brazil or in Asia, it will always have the same fragrance, the same concentration, the same presentation. This is an eau de parfum extreme, so a little bit of it goes a long way.

Dupes are perfumes inspired by a designer perfume. As the exact recipe of a fragrance is a secret, something even protected by law, the dupes bring an olfactory reference to the original. So a dupe of this perfume here, will remind me of the original, but it won't be exactly the same, it won't have the same presentation and it may also have a different concentration. There are people who are absolutely against such products, others use them a lot, mainly because sometimes the designer perfumes are very expensive.

For me, a good quality dupe can be a good option when you really want a perfume but you can't buy it at the moment. I see it as a democratization of perfume. This perfume here is Invictus Victory by Pacco Rabane, that costs almost half of the minimum wage here in brazil. It's not something the average consumer will buy all the time here, right? But be careful because there are dupes of different quality. That's why it's good for you to learn how to make perfumes, because you can make your dupes or artisan perfumes knowing exactly the quality and origin of each material.

While the dupe "imitates" the smell of the original, the counterfeit aims to imitate the packaging, name, color and other characteristics of the product to pass for the original. This is a totally illegal practice. Counterfeit perfumes can be very harmful to health because imagine that if the person is trying to trick you into buying a fake while paying the cost of the original, they don't care about the quality of what they put in that bottle.

Here you will learn everything you need to know to create your fragrance from scratch, but if you want to make your dupes, that's fine. What you will create and what ingredients you will use is totally up to you, this course will not chain you and force you to make just one type of perfume. With the knowledge you are acquiring here, creativity will be your limit.

blocks.text: AROMA FUNDAMENTALS
Train your Nose

To make perfume, it is helpful to know some of the fundamentals and traditions of fragrance design. This section here covers three main topics: fragrance families, notes and aromatic blends. But before anything else I need to explain to you the importance of training your sense of smell.
When I tell people who don't know me that I'm an aromatherapist, the first thing they say is "you must have a very good nose" or "you must be very sensitive to smells".
I don't believe I have a better sense of smell than anyone else, but I'm a very good communicator (because I'm a teacher) and I have a good memory - this is key, along with years of training.

Perfumery is essentially about perception, creation and communication of scents, and while the nose is used as a tool, it is nothing without the brain. Most of us are able to perceive odors, but many people find it difficult to describe and communicate what they are smelling in a way that others can understand.

This is the fundamental point that I need you to understand. A perfumer must know his materials extremely well and be able to recognize, describe and mix them together to create something else, a new scent.

When we are children, we learn how to speak by recognizing people, images, objects and repeating the names or words attributed to these people, images, objects, etc. Right? We look for visual cues such as color and shape, also texture and, to some extent, the sounds we hear and the emotions we feel.
Our sense of smell is different. It has existed since before speech. Long before our vocabulary develops, we already feel the aromas that at that moment in life are closely linked to taste.
We learn over time to intuitively identify things by smell, but we never learn the words to communicate them until they are related to a familiar object, such as an orange, a baby food, a shampoo.
For adults it is more difficult to learn things by repetition, especially when we want to rationalize and rush too much of what is being learned.
But smell works on such a subjective level that it's especially difficult to learn about fragrance materials in this way, because our perception and memory of odors varies from person to person.

When you train your nose to recognize specific odors and materials, you are actually training your brain. Forget reading odor, aroma and fragrance descriptions - start sniffing the materials and write your own thoughts in a notebook.

This way you will create your own links and associations with memories, feelings, colors and textures. By practicing regularly and methodically, you will build your olfactory memory, which will make your work much easier in the future.
Introduction to the Fragrance Wheel

What a color wheel is to understand colors, the fragrance wheel is to categorize different scents. The wheel is a circular diagram that indicates similarities and differences between various "olfactory flavors".

The fragrance wheel was created in 1949 by Paul Jellinek, an Austrian perfumer. The first mention of the fragrance wheel was made in Jellinek's book "Practice of Modern Perfumery". The wheel was called the "Odor Effects Diagram" at the time.

However, the wheel has gone through many evolutions since then. In 1979, U. Harder created the "Scented Circle", in 1984 Ann C. Nobel reinvented the wheel as the "Wine Aroma Wheel". The modern fragrance wheel is inspired by Michael Edwards' reimagining of the wheel from 1992.

So fragrance wheels are used for multitude purposes. The idea is that it serves as a guide to create combinations from popular aromatic notes. That is, the fragrance wheel serves as a tool to identify different olfactory notes, especially when combining two or more scents.

The aromas that appear side by side on the wheel have common traits that blend easily with each other. For example, Floral Oriental, Soft Oriental and Oriental appear linked to each other because they have similar olfactory notes.
On the other hand, opposite fragrances on the wheel have contrasting characteristics. For example, Dry wood is the opposite of the scent found in Soft Floral.

But you can't forget one thing: creativity has no limits. The fragrance wheel serves as a guide to help you experiment with blending scents. Truly creative perfumers can successfully create a new fragrance without using the wheel and using contrasting or similar notes. It all comes down to personal taste and a lot of testing.

Later in the course I will show you how I created a fragrance inspired by my grandmother, where I used more of my creativity to reach the final result. So, you can use the fragrance wheel to experiment, test and creat but don't allow it or any tool to stop your creativity.
The Olfactory Families

Olfactory Families are like categories on the Fragrance Wheel. Each family is a coalition of aromas with similar traits and characteristics. Therefore, fragrances from a family appear next to each other on the wheel.

pages.title: Olfactory families: oriental, floral and fresh

blocks.text: A typical fragrance wheel is divided into four sections or families. These families are - Oriental, Floral, Fresh and Woody. So, all aromas that are part of a certain family, have similar aromatic notes.

Interestingly, each family can be divided into aroma subgroups. Each subgroup has something extra that the other subgroups don't. However, all subgroups within a family share the same basic scents. For example, specific olfactory notes in a Floral scent create the Soft Floral subgroup.

Another interesting thing is that olfactory subgroups from different families can share common traits if they are neighbors on the fragrance wheel. For example, Aromatic belongs to the Fresh family, while Dry Woods is part of the Woody family. But as they are next to each other on the fragrance wheel, they share some typical notes despite belonging to different families.
Let's have a better understanding of these families and their subgroups?
Oriental Notes

The first family of fragrances is Oriental which you can also find as amber in some wheels. Many perfumers prefer oriental notes due to its sweet aroma. In addition to the sugary aroma, oriental fragrances are associated with sophistication and richness. Think of all the exotic and sensual scents - they perfectly describe oriental aromas.
Some popular scents in this family include vanilla, orchid, cinnamon and cardamom. The subgroups in oriental notes are:
Floral Oriental - As the name suggests, this subgroup has the richness of the Oriental and the freshness of the Floral notes. Think sweet spices and orange blossom.
Soft Oriental - As the name suggests, these notes have a certain lightness in their aroma, they are inspiring notes like frankincense and star anise.
Oriental - Aromas in this category are identified by their deep musky scent. Some of the notes in this category include resins, vanilla, cinnamon and other spices.
Woody Oriental - These notes have warmth and an earthy quality. They are scents like patchouli and sandalwood that bring rich, dense and cozy notes.
Floral Notes

Many people associate Floral fragrances with feminine qualities or with delicate and subtle aromas. However, don't be fooled, with the right combinations, floral scents can become complex and sophisticated very far from being delicate.
The subgroups in Floral Notes are:
Floral - Freshness is the focus here. Notes in the floral family can range from spicy and bright like lily to light and woody like rose.
Soft Floral - The soft Floral notes are famous for very light aromas that resemble the scent of baby powder.
Fresh Notes

In this family citrus and herbal aromas bring energy and vitality to any environment. In terms of notes, fresh aromas are the most diverse of all, bringing together notes extracted in various ways in nature.
The subgroups in Fresh notes are:
Fruity - Fruity aromas are sweeter and rounder. Apples, pears, peaches, strawberries and tropical fruits bring radiance and youth to this subgroup.
Green — Green aromas are fresh and slightly woody. Galbanum is a great example of this subgroup.
Water - Here you will find notes that remind you of the marine aroma, of the ocean breeze, of algae.
Citrus - As the name suggests, citrus aromas are bright and spicy. You find these notes in orange, bergamot, lemon... in other words, citrus are very easy to remember.

pages.title: Woody notes and using the wheel

blocks.text: Aromatic - Also found as herbal, these notes are known for their seductive and energizing aroma. Here you can find the aromas of aromatic herbs and some camphor flowers, such as lavender.
Woody Notes

The Woody aroma comprises not only aromatic notes that we relate to wood, but also earthy notes. They are aromas with a deep, earthy character. Typically, woody notes are used to balance other brighter or softer notes because they add weight to the overall fragrance.
The subgroups in Woody Notes are:
Woods - Warm and mysterious, woods notes are the "basic" type of woody scent that is often the most popular type of modern masculine fragrances.
Mossy Woods - Also known as Musk, these notes bring green and woody aromas, they were a basic and popular perfume type in classic men's perfume during the 70's and 80's.
Dry Woods - They are purer and drier woody notes, in current perfumery they bring a somewhat new style.
You can also find Woody Oriental as a subgroup in Woody notes in some Fragrance Wheels. But this is not a problem.

Remember that the idea of the Wheel is to help you better categorize scents and, thus, use them in a more organized and coherent way. However, it is not restrictive, that is, it is very much up to the person who is using it to follow it or not. Furthermore you may disagree that a certain scent is in a certain subgroup.

I myself have seen books that consider Star Anise as Soft Oriental and others that consider it Floral Oriental. In the end, creating a fragrance that is pleasant to wear and that pleases people is what matters, so these discussions become a waste of time, we gain much more by testing and using our creativity.
How to Use the Fragrance Wheel

As I said earlier, the Fragrance Wheel can be very helpful for beginners, but there are no right or wrong answers when blending scents. It all comes down to your personal taste and the purpose of the fragrance you are creating.

It's interesting to think - at what time of day will this new fragrance be worn? Is it to be used in a more casual moment or for a more special moment? What kind of feeling or sensation do you want to evoke with this fragrance? Answering questions like these can help you find the right notes.

For example, a perfume to be worn during the day on a social occasion. A combination of something citrusy and fruity with a hint of woody oriental can be interesting. The citrus and fruity aroma adds a little freshness and blends in with daytime wear. At the same time, the oriental woody fragrance will help adding weight and sophistication to the overall scent. At least that's what I would do, you can have different ideas and combinations.

I understand that when we're starting out this can be tricky because it's all very new and confusing. That's why in this lecture I'm going to give you important tips on how to use the fragrance wheel when starting out, getting the best out of it.
1. It is interesting to test blends of fragrances from opposite families on the wheel.

Once you've decided on the scent family and subgroup you want to start this new fragrance with, mix your note with a note on the other side of the wheel. This contrast often leaves an impression of complexity and brings out incredibly balanced aromas.

notes: The book uses “base” here to mean the foundation of a composition, not necessarily the base-note layer.

blocks.text: 2. When you want to create a strong and unique scent base, combine and test scents next to each other on the fragrance wheel. That is, the notes are slightly similar, which will give you that stronger base.
3. For a remarkable olfactory experience, you can use triangulated subgroups.
This means mixing fragrances that form a triangle on the wheel. For example - Citrus, Soft Floral and Woody Oriental create a triangle. This combination can result in a very interesting fragrance.

blocks.caption: Original triangle illustration connecting Citrus, Soft Floral and Woody Oriental.

blocks.text: 4. Improve your knowledge of different types of scents and their impact.
You may have already noticed that the Fragrance Wheel is quite general. You need to familiarize yourself with the scents
included in each family and subgroup. This of course takes time, but this learning time will save you precious time down the road when you're creating something new.

To help you get started you know that you have the booklet with 55 recipes for Artisan fragrances, and of course you can start by following them, or change them during your tests. And then I advise you to test and create your own fragrances from scratch.
5. Open up to new scents.

While we all have a favorite scent that we can't get enough of, it's nice to open up and try new things. You never know which unique combination might become your new favorite. I myself couldn't stand the scent of Ylang Ylang before and today it is one of the scents that I find most interesting.

Lastly, take it slow, control your anxiety. Don't mix a dozen notes at once when testing. You could end up with a messy, characterless blend. Granted there are perfumes that contain more than 20 notes, but all fragrances are built little by little, adding one note at a time, testing, modifying and adding other notes slowly.
The Olfactory Pyramid

Perfumes are, in essence, a fusion of many different chemical compounds that we recognize as scents. Both synthetic and natural ingredients are used to create a balanced and striking fragrance. Most perfumers do not disclose the exact composition, the formula of a perfume. At most today, the scents used are presented and that a person with a trained sense of smell would be able to identify.
As you may have noticed when I talked about Olfactory Families, the word 'notes' is used to refer to these ingredients with similar aromas. In perfumery the notes merge to create olfactory accords.

If you are someone who pays attention to details, you may have noticed that the scent of perfumes on your body changes throughout the day. While this may be surprising at first, it's an important factor to look out for when you're creating your own fragrance.

Each note has a different level of volatility, which is why the overall fragrance changes subtly throughout the day. The volatility of a perfume's different notes determines how it dries on the skin and evaporates over time.

pages.title: Top, heart and base notes

blocks.text: Due to the heat of our skin, a fragrance dries slowly when we apply it and then starts to slowly evaporate. That's when something, which appears to be quite magical, happens. Different compounds evaporate at different rates due to their varying chemical compositions. The scent changes a little each time a batch of 'notes' evaporates. If all the notes evaporated at the same time, you wouldn't be able to smell it afterwards.

Thus, it is possible to say that each perfume has a life cycle. Notes that can be immediately identified generally tend to be highly volatile and evaporate quickly. These are the top notes, also called the head notes.
However, they are immediately replaced by other notes, called heart notes, which diffuse into the perfume, maintaining its charm. Heart notes can also be called middle notes.
The last layer of notes, known as base notes, generally last longer and ensure the scent stays on the skin as long as possible.

This makes it easy to understand the life cycle of a fragrance, it simply goes through the succession of notes to reach the point where it finally disappears completely. That said, the composition of a fragrance can determine the nature of transitions. Thinking and using different notes in your creation will ensure that your perfume not only has memorable aromatic chords but will also help to maintain the aroma for a longer period of time on the body. A fragrance made with only top notes will soon fade, no matter how much fixative you use in your recipe.
Notes are usually represented in a pyramid, the olfactory pyramid. Which is a simple but effective tool to convey the life cycle of a fragrance.
Top Notes: 5-15 minutes

A perfume's top notes, placed at the top of the pyramid, tend to be the most memorable and vivid for any wearer. They're pretty much the immediate scent we get when spraying a perfume, which means they're key to forming the first impression of any perfume. However, these notes are also the most volatile, so they evaporate the fastest. As they have smaller, lighter molecules, they bounce off the skin after imparting a burst of fragrance. They last for the first 5 to 15 minutes after spraying a perfume.
However, the importance of the top notes is undeniable because they help orchestrate a transition to the second layer, composed of the heart notes.
Heart Notes: 20-60 minutes

The heart notes become more evident as the top notes evaporate and remain evident for about 20 minutes to a full hour. Often referred to as the 'soul' of the perfume, these middle notes create a perfect bridge between the other layers of the perfume. They tend to make up the personality of a fragrance and are evident in the evolution of the perfume even after evaporation. One of the most functional aspects of heart notes is that they help suppress base notes until they are ripe enough to emerge and complement the fragrance. They hold the top notes a little bit and slowly introduce the base notes so the user doesn't have a jarring experience.
Base notes: 5-6 hours

The base notes are responsible for holding the perfume's fragrance together as the top and middle notes evaporate. Once the middle notes penetrate the base notes, they mature enough to emerge and add depth to the scent. The base of each perfume is based on its range of base notes, because this layer lasts longer in the fragrance's life cycle, 5-6 hours minimum. These notes slowly start to appear while the middle notes are evident and then carry the scent forward creating unique accords. They tend to be rich, heavy and grounded so the scent can stay on the skin longer.

In Aromatherapy we use the Olfactory Pyramid with a simple rule, called 30-50-20, where we create a blend of essential oils with 30% top notes, 50% heart notes and 20% base notes. The idea of this mathematical rule is to give a proportion to the aroma while taking advantage of the different volatility rates of the notes. Of course it's not mandatory, but I like to use it when I'm

notes: Timing ranges and 30 / 50 / 20 are the instructor’s illustrative model, not fixed behavior for every blend.

pages.title: Using the pyramid and the 30 / 50 / 20 idea

blocks.text: creating a fragrance from scratch because it helps me in the process, but I'm always testing and often I don't keep these proportions.

You might be thinking: OK, but how do I know when a certain aroma is top, middle, or base note? In addition to the descriptions I've given in this lecture, you can google it or use an essential oil profile book or website. A very trusted one is called Aromaweb (https://www.aromaweb.com/), this website has more than 100 essential oils profiles. But remember that no list is complete and there may be differences from one list to another. This is common because scents are very subjective.

But anyway, you can also use this image as a guide, which will be available in the ebook with the transcripts of the lectures. In it you see that most of the fresh notes are top notes: Water, Citrus and Aromatic. The middle notes include the two last aromas of the fresh family (fruity and green) and all the floral and oriental notes. And, finally, at the base are the woody aromas and also the balsamic ones like vanilla and resins.

While effective in helping us, the perfume pyramid is not perfect. It serves as a great structure to visually convey the composition of a fragrance, so we are more aware of the life cycle of the perfume we are creating.

Previously, most perfumes adopted this three-layer model, but now perfumes have varied structures and there is no one right rule or one single recipe. You can create fragrances that maintain the pyramid structure, or create fragrances that have more than three layers.

blocks.text: It's a great idea to start with, as is the use of the Fragrance Wheel, but with practice and tests you end up developing your own way of making fragrances and making these models simpler and that in a way are easy to replicate.
Developing Fragrances
While it is possible to make single-note perfumes (that is, perfumes with only one scent), it is much more common and better to mix different scents. In fact, that's the fun part! But where to start?
Well, scents from the same category usually go well together.
And it's also good to try to get at least a top note to elevate the scent, a base note to ground it, and a heart note to tie the two together - plus, follow your tastes and your nose!
You can create using the Fragrance Wheel as a start or you can also try the basic and ready-made recipes that I provide in the resources and then change them.

Creating fragrances is part art and part science, as I said. While it is helpful for you to familiarize yourself with the olfactory families, fragrance notes and how they interact, it is certainly not necessary. What is needed is a creative drive and an adventurous spirit.

Start by testing each note on a labeled scent strip. You can then combine notes by joining the strips and making it like a fan, fanning to smell, then adding and removing strips until you get the desired combination.
When you decide to blend the fragrance, start with the base notes as they are the strongest. Then add the heart notes and finally the top notes.

Start with a few drops of the aroma at a time and keep track of the number of drops! Write down your recipes so you can recreate them later. On the next lecture I will show you how I created the fragrance that I presented at the end of a Perfumery Masterclass in London, the story behind this fragrance ended up earning me the award for best creation in the class.
The Perfumer's Palette

When master perfumers start creating a new fragrance, they have approximately 3,000 aromatics to work with. Five hundred of them are natural raw materials and the remaining 25 hundred are synthetic materials. Of course, you don't need all that to start your creations. But, little by little, you must create your own palette.

You may have noticed in my demo that it all starts with a briefing which is basically a description of what we want: who the target customer is, what the fragrance's mood should be, what time it will be used, etc. This gives the perfumer a clear idea of what they are looking for.

Of course, every perfumer has their favorite ingredients and we can always go back to certain notes or scents over and over again. It becomes your signature. I, for example, always include a citrus touch or an oriental touch.

An average modern perfume today contains anywhere from 20 to 100 aromatics. Of these, six to eight define the perfume's personality. Many are used in small amounts to properly stabilize or balance the fragrance or give it a certain nuanced note.
My suggestion is that you start with ready-made recipes and create your Aromatic Palette, then you test and create your fragrances.

blocks.text: PERFUME FUNDAMENTALS
Perfume Materials

There are several ways to make perfumes. In this section I will cover the materials used in making Artisan Perfumes as some materials used in store bought perfumes are only available for big industries. I'll also talk about the various types of perfumes. For each material presented I'l discuss its strengths, weaknesses and usefulness.
Simply put, perfume is made up of a fragrance and a base - this base is the material to which the fragrance is added. This is what we call a "carrier” because it carries the aroma.
A base is necessary because many fragrances are very strong and sometimes not safe in direct contact with the skin. So this base performs a triple function that I will talk about later.

The second most common component of perfume is the fragrance or aromatic. An aromatic can come from natural sources, such as essential oils and absolutes, or from synthetic sources, such as scented oils and other aromatic chemicals.

Some people have strong opinions about using natural or synthetic products in their perfumes. As essential oils and absolutes can be very expensive to make perfumes, I'm going to talk about using both and you can decide what you prefer for your perfumes.
Fragrance

The perfume market boomed with the mid 19th century Industrial Revolution when synthetic chemicals were introduced in their manufacture, before that perfumes weren't really accessible to the general public. Today, the art of perfume making has become a global multi-billion industry, and the perfume making process has gone through many refinements and improvements over the decades.

Modern perfume manufacturers prefer synthetic chemicals over natural oils, although natural ingredients are still highly prized for use in the finest and most expensive perfumes. This shift has also been good for consumers, as the use of synthetics has driven down the price of perfumes and encouraged more frequent use of scents in the everyday life of the average user.
Synthetic Aromas

I believe that here in the course I already said that most perfumes on the market today are made from a combination of natural and synthetic materials. The most basic form of ingredient is synthetic aroma. It is essentially a blend of aromatic chemicals, made in a laboratory.
These synthetic aromas can be identical to nature or they can be invented by humans.

Most commercial perfume fragrances today carry about 70% to 100% of synthetics. And that's not a bad thing. If all synthetics were switched to naturally sourced ingredients, supply would not be able to keep up with demand, making the entire perfumery industry utterly unsustainable. We also need to understand that when it comes to perfumes, aromas made in the laboratory are more ecological than naturally derived ones, precisely because they do not depend on natural resources.

pages.title: Fragrance oils, essential oils and absolutes

blocks.text: This is quite different from Aromatherapy, which is the therapeutic use of aromas. In Aromatherapy we need 100% natural ingredients because the goal is different. Also, a high concentration of essential oils in perfumes can cause allergy or other skin problems.
Fragrance Oils

Fragrance Oils are typically a combination of synthetic and natural substances, in candle making they are often referred to as Premium Fragrances. It is important to be clear that they are not simply essential oils diluted in an oil base. Both fragrance Oils and essential oils are called that because they have properties similar to, but they are not really oils, because if they were oils in the strict sense of the word they would never mix with the perfume base.

Through these fragrances you can obtain scents that cannot be extracted naturally, such as Lily, or replicate scents that are usually very expensive, such as rose or amber. Because they are synthetically made, Fragrance Oils also tend to cost less than essential oils and have fewer rules regarding proper storage and protection. However, fragrance oils vary in cost depending on the price of the ingredients used to make them. Also, as with so many other things, price is often a reflection of quality.
Essential oils

Well known and highly sought after for their therapeutic properties, essential oils can be used in the creation of organic perfumes, that is 100% natural fragrances, and are often part of blends with synthetics in expensive perfumes. As this is not an aromatherapy course, I will not delve too deeply into the many possible uses of this raw material. But I need to draw attention to some points of use of essential oils.

As they are a very concentrated raw material, they should not be placed directly on skin, as this can cause serious health complications. Some essential oils, particularly those from citrus fruits, can cause photosensitivity, which makes the skin very sensitive to sunlight. Although the amounts of essential oils used in perfumes are very small, still pay attention to where the perfume is applied, as this area can become more reactive when exposed to sunlight.
Some essential oils should not be used during pregnancy, in people who are very young, old, or have other health conditions. My suggestion is never to use an essential oil without studying it first.
Absolutes

While most essential oils are extracted by steam distillation or cold pressing, absolutes are created by solvent extraction. One of the first challenges faced by early perfumers was that some organic products are too delicate for steam distillation. An excellent example of this is Jasmine. To extract Jasmine's scent, one should use less aggressive techniques, extracting the fragrance slowly.

The most traditional version of this extraction method is enfleurage. In enfleurage, the flowers are arranged on a tray with some fat. The fat will slowly extract the scent as the petals die. This process is repeated until the fat is saturated. If it stays as it is, it's called "ointment". If, however, we incorporate alcohol, the fragrance molecules will move out of the fat. Once the fat separates, it gives away its scent to the alcohol. Then the alcohol is evaporated resulting in the "absolute" fragrance.

However, enfleurage is a time-consuming method that has been rendered obsolete by modern science. Nowadays, we can use solvents to extract the scented particles and then distill them into a waxy solid called concrete. This concrete is then treated: the ethyl alcohol is mixed, then separated and

pages.title: Absolutes, carriers and alcohol

blocks.text: evaporated - leaving behind the precious absolute.

Because the solvent extraction process is more delicate, absolutes often carry aromas that are "truer" to the original plant than essential oils. They generally smell fresher than essential oils and are preferred by many natural perfumers over essential oils.

However, it is also common for absolutes to carry traces of the solvent used to extract them - often impacting the aroma. That's why aromatherapists tend to prefer essential oils. The best absolutes are those extracted using CO2, they do not have residual aroma and are widely used both in aromatherapy and in perfumery, maintaining the natural quality of fragrances.
In terms of price, Absolutes tend to be more expensive than essential oils.
Carriers
I've told you a perfume is made of more than just fragrance. Once the fragrance formula is conceived, these aromatics are added to a carrier – a base material that "carries" the perfume.

The carrier has three functions and the most important one is to protect the user. Many essential oils, absolutes and scented oils are potentially harmful when applied directly to skin. They can be mildly caustic, contain allergens, affect the way sunlight interacts with our skin, be irritating, cause rashes, etc. In addition, essential oils often have effects on the body based on the nature of the plant from which they are derived. While some effects are positive, such as the healing power of lavender, even good things can be bad in large doses. Diluting these raw materials in a carrier makes these problems disappear.

That's why I recommended it, and here's a reminder that before using any oil as a key ingredient in your perfumes, it's important that you study its specific properties and also that you test the perfume on your skin.

The second function is to give reach and fixation to the perfume. That is, the base you use will influence the duration of a perfume and the range at which others can smell it. For example, an alcohol base has a much wider range because the alcohol evaporates and takes some of the fragrance with it. On the other hand, an oil base will set the scent on your skin better because the oil penetrates the pores and evaporates more slowly.

The third and final function of the carrier is to dilute the fragrance. Yes, because many scents in fragrances are quite pungent on their own; the scent is often too strong to use neat - even if the fragrance ingredients are safe.
Carriers can also be called bases and the three most common bases for perfumes are alcohol, oil and wax.
Alcohol

Alcohol is the most common perfume base. To completely dissolve the compounds in a fragrance, we need good, pure ethyl alcohol. The higher the alcohol content, the greater the clarity of the perfume, that is: a low alcohol content produces a grainy, muddy and uninteresting perfume.

So what's the solution? Many artisan perfumers turn to high-quality vodka. Some will say that ethyl alcohol is also a good carrier because it doesn't have a scent of its own. Others strongly insist that alcohol has a smell.
Anyway, when you make a perfume with alcohol, the carrier is the first to evaporate. After a few seconds, all that is left is the fragrance itself.

pages.title: Oils, waxes and fixatives

blocks.text: Another option for alcohol-based perfumes is the ready-made perfume base. It's basically a preparation that also sometimes has other ingredients, such as an emulsifier (something that helps the oils and alcohol mix), an emollient (which is a thickening agent), or a fixative (which extends the life of the fragrance).

A note of caution: alcohol is flammable, and the purer the alcohol, the more flammable it is. So when entering the perfume business, it is interesting to study the legislation where you live, with the rules you must follow in relation to the shipping or sale of alcohol-based perfumes.
Oils and Waxes

It is possible to use an oil or combinations of oils when making perfumes. The most commonly used oils are jojoba, fractionated coconut and sunflower oil, mainly because these oils are almost odorless. However, you can create your products using oils of your choice as long as the scent satisfies you. Waxes can also be used in the making of solid perfumes and the most suitable is beeswax.
It can be found in natural pieces or in refined tablet form. The most recommended is the use of refined beeswax, because it is a material that has been purified of any residue from the honeycomb.
We will delve a little deeper into the issue of carriers in the practical lessons.
Fixatives

This is a somewhat controversial subject in Perfumery, some say that they are unnecessary or that if you use a ready-made perfume base, you don't need to understand about fixatives because "the work has already been done for you". But the objective of the course is for you to learn and be able to create your perfumes, so it is necessary to have a better understanding of what fixatives really are and how they work in perfume compositions.
Let's first understand the characteristics and functions of fixatives in perfumery:
1. They decrease the rate of evaporation of the more volatile materials in perfume composition, causing gradual changes in the perfume's aroma as the ingredients evaporate;
2. Fixatives better stabilize, fortify and transport aromas by providing a combination of diffusion and retentive effect.
3. They are odorless or almost odorless, so they do not change the final scent of the perfume.

But a fixative isn't the only thing that helps keep the scent on our skin longer. Perfume fixation is also related to base notes. Remember when we talked about the Olfactory Pyramid and I said that the base notes are denser components that are difficult to volatilize, which act to release the scents more slowly.

Another factor that contributes to the fixation of perfume is the concentration of the fragrance. The concentration of aromatics varies according to the concentration of the perfume. We'll learn about this classification in the next lecture, and you'll see that the higher the fragrance concentration is, the stronger the scent will last.

notes: The source presents a general explanation of fixatives; different products can have their own odor and behavior.

blocks.text: Something that should also be taken into account when evaluating the fixation of a perfume is the skin type. Yes, the skin type will also determine the fixation, as the skin is the base that absorbs the fragrance.
Dry skin tends to retain less perfume due to lack of hydration. Therefore, it is recommended to moisturize the skin with a neutral moisturizer before applying perfume.
Normal skin has a more homogeneous texture, with balanced hydration and oiliness, the average perfume fixation can reach more than eight hours depending on the perfume concentration.

Oily skin is best for perfume fixation, an Eau de Toilette fragrance can last between eight and twelve hours here. However, some care should be doubled for those who tend to have severe headaches and allergies, as the absorption of perfume in this type of skin is even greater.

It is important to keep in mind that many times, when we think that the perfume has evaporated from our skin, the truth is that we have gotten used to the aroma and that is why we think the perfume is weak. However, this has nothing to do with perfume fixation, this is called Olfactory Saturation or Olfactory Accommodation and is related to our perception of the fragrance and not the product fixation itself.
But it's no use buying an expensive fixative or a base that says it has the best fixative if you don't have a balanced and good quality perfume fragrance.
Liquid Perfume Concentration
Liquid perfume is by far the most popular and well-known form of perfume. They fall into two categories: alcohol-based and oil-based.

The industry uses special terms according to the perfume's concentration ratio and the gender of the wearer. However, these terms aren't standardized and people usually don't pay much attention to them.

For example, many feel that the difference between perfume and cologne is based on the gender of the wearer. That is, women wear perfume and men wear cologne. But actually perfumes tend to be more floral and more potent, while colognes tend to be more musky and softer.

But, going back to the concentration ratio, traditionally the different types of liquid perfumes are given different names according to their aromatics percentage. Here I'm going to talk in general, because the actual concentration rates vary a little from producer to producer.
Body Splash and Body Spray

These are the lightest products, containing around 1-3% aromatics. It is usually called a splash when marketed to men and a spray when marketed to women. In addition, as the English names indicate, splashes are sold in bottles with an opening so that men can apply the fragrance, while body sprays are sold in bottles with a spray cap.
Cologne

It may contain 4-7% aromatic compounds. This name is also often used to distinguish men's fragrances and is traditionally made with citrus oils or lighter, more refreshing scents. It has a fast evaporation rate and lasts a few hours on the body.
Eau de Toilette

It contains 7-10% aromatic compounds. A curious thing is that Eau de Toilette was originally used in gloves and scarves, not as something applied to the skin. They are generally versatile fragrances that can be used at any time of the day. It lasts about 8 hours on the body.
Eau de Parfum
It contains 10-20% aromatic compounds. More common among women's fragrances, but increasingly seen in men's fragrances as well. It lasts for up to 10 hours on the body.
Parfum

It may contain 20-40% aromatic compounds. Those with 20% are the easiest to find, but there are Arab perfumes that reach 40% aromatics. The parfum is luxurious and the most expensive variant of any fragrance family, in addition to providing a longevity of at least 12 hours. But it should be used in moderation, due to the high content of aromatics.

blocks.text: Solid Perfumes

Perfume in solid form is not that common. But it has been gaining fans, for the practicality of use and for being much more natural. To use solid perfumes just rub your finger in the perfume, the heat of your body will make the perfume melt slightly. You apply the perfume on your body and that's it!

Solid perfumes are easy to make, they can be packed in compact containers, and are easily transported. The biggest downside to using solid perfume is the tendency for it to melt in a warm environment.

They should not be left in trouser pockets, hot cars, or direct sunlight, as the mixture will melt and become a runny mess, often leaking out of the container. Of course, when the product cools down, it will solidify again, but in the meantime it causes that mess.
I'll talk a little more about these perfumes before the hands-on lecture, but you can start thinking about this possibility too.
EQUIPMENT AND SAFETY
Equipment
You don't need a lot of equipment to make perfume, even if you already make something like candles and cosmetics, chances are you already have a lot of the necessary equipment.

If you're going to use essential oils and absolutes, it's best to wear gloves. Pure essential oils and absolutes can cause skin allergies or even minor burns, so it's important that you always take care not to have these problems.
Also, it's nice to have goggles if you don't wear glasses like I do, because your eyes are protected in case you accidentally cause a little disaster.

To test your fragrances, it's a good idea to have scent strips or some kind of paper or cotton wool that absorbs the scents quickly and allows you to smell it. You've seen in my demo where I was creating a fragrance that scent strips help when trying out blends to make sure they smell like you're expecting.

Glass droppers or pipettes are important as they work very well to control the amount of aromatics you are adding to a blend, it is much better to have them too when you are going to make a fragrance in large quantities. It is interesting that it is glass because essential and absolute oils can degrade plastic and rubber.

You will also need a glass container to mix the oils, it can be a beaker. It all depends on how much you are going to use. Also, it is important to have a storage container to allow the blends to cure. Again, both should be glass, and the storage container should be amber or dark blue to avoid exposure to light, particularly if you use essential oils in your fragrance.

As I make perfumes only as a hobby I use the milliliter markings of the beakers or pipettes themselves. If you intend to do it in larger quantities, it might be interesting to study the need for a scale and then use weight instead of milliliters. But nothing is mandatory.

Of course you will need a bottle to put your perfume in. It depends on your taste and creativity, you can use a glass spray bottle, an old perfume bottle, a roll-on glass container and, in the case of solid perfume, I suggest a can with a lid. All of this can be easily found online if you can't find it where you live.

You may also need a funnel to pour the finished perfume into the bottle. If you are making solid perfumes you will need an enameled pan (if like me you use an electric stove) or a double boiler. It could be the same pan you use to make candles, if you do. But remember that this pan can never be used to cook.

Labels are easily forgotten. Be sure to label not only your perfume bottles, but also bottles with your scents and the bottles where you let the fragrances cure. Cheap labels are not hard to find, and you can opt for a more practical solution like a labeling machine, depending on your investment conditions and needs.

Now, one important thing that is not equipment is: you should also have a notebook to write down all your fragrance recipes that you have developed. Trust me and not your memory - write everything down so you don't end up creating a wonderful fragrance and then barely remembering the ingredients or their amounts!

pages.title: Health, safety and regulatory aspects

blocks.text: Health and Safety

Wearing gloves and goggles when dealing with essential oils, absolutes and synthetics may seem unnecessary, but remember that these aromatics are concentrated and only after being diluted does their concentration become harmless.

Try not to inhale the aromatics straight from the bottle - to test the scent, simply add a drop to the scent strip. It is also interesting not to sniff aromatics for a long time - it will be difficult to assess the smell later, when the nose "gets used" to it. You can use coffee beans to "restart" your nose.
Furthermore:
• Do not smoke and avoid open flames or other potential sources of ignition near where you are working, remember that everything is flammable.
• Wash your hands well after using aromatics.
• Work in rooms with good ventilation.
Store aromatics in closed containers, away from heat sources.
• Always keep ingredients out of the reach of children or animals.

If an aromatic comes into contact with your skin - remove contaminated clothing, wash your skin with plenty of water and a mild soap. If irritation persists or skin damage is visible, seek medical attention immediately.
If an aromatic or base gets in your eyes, wash your eyes with plenty of water for at least 10 minutes. Seek medical attention if irritation persists or if there is immediate damage.
If you've inhaled a lot of the fragrance and you're not feeling well - step outside for some fresh air, and rest. See a doctor immediately if symptoms do not improve.
Particularly sensitive people should be more careful.
Regulatory Aspects
In Brazil the production of cosmetics for personal use is allowed. But to market, it is necessary to seek governmental approval.
If your intention is to market the products you make, it is interesting for you to start researching and analyzing all the requirements to do so in your country.

Regulatory aspects are important to ensure consumer health, as there is a big difference between making a cosmetic for your own use and marketing it. It needs to be safe so as not to compromise the health of anyone using it.

From the beginning, you can make sure that your perfume complies with the IFRA - International Fragrance Association. IFRA is the self-regulatory body of the international fragrance industry and was created to help fragrance creators produce safe perfumes.
Compliance with IFRA is voluntary and you do not need to become a member to comply with its regulations. Even if you are not considering selling your perfumes, I advise any serious perfume

blocks.text: LIQUID PERFUMES
Choosing a Carrier

So we come to a question I've heard a lot: what is the best carrier for a fragrance, alcohol or vegetable oil? Well, that depends on your tastes and what you expect from the perfume because oils and alcohols interact very differently with fragrant materials, basically delivering two different products.

If you don't want to use alcohol and prefer to use vegetable oil, you must remember that in a perfume of this type the scent will have a smaller reach, that is, the people around you will only feel this aroma if they get very close. The range of the scent can increase with your body heat. Also, unlike alcohol that dries out the skin, oil-based perfumes are hydrating.
Since oil adheres to the skin better than alcohol, the scent will stay with you longer; But remember that what you gain in longevity, you lose in range.

The most used oil as a perfume base is fractionated coconut oil. This is coconut oil that has been modified to remain liquid at room temperature and has no aroma that could interfere with the final fragrance. Additionally, Fractionated Coconut Oil is noticeably thinner, leaving a less greasy residue on the skin than most vegetable oils and has an indefinite shelf life.
But it's also important to remember that if you want to spray your perfume, the oil will not serve as a base. In that case you should use an alcohol base.
In chemistry it is possible to say that there can be an almost infinite number of alcohols. Cedrol is an example that is found naturally in cedar essential oil.

But for perfumery, the alcohol used is ethanol. Ethanol is found everywhere; from alcoholic beverages to biofuels, in addition to perfume. In fact, ethanol is so common that the term "alcohol" is used in everyday life to refer to it.

But of course there are several types of alcohols in the family called Ethanol. Choosing which "alcohol" to buy to make perfumes often causes confusion among beginning perfumers, and if you've searched online what alcohol to add to your perfume, you may have encountered some of this terms:
•Perfumer's alcohol or perfume base
•Isopropyl Alcohol
•Grain alcohol
•Vodka
•Witch hazel Extract
•Methanol
Shall we understand each of them?
Perfumer's alcohol or perfume base

Perfume base is a mixture of alcohol and some common additives such as water and fixative, which facilitate the production of perfume. It's okay to use a perfume base, because creating your base from scratch requires

pages.title: Comparing carriers and preparing a base

blocks.text: investing a little more in other products and you can often get the proportions wrong or you may not like the final product, mainly because depending on where you live, finding good quality materials is difficult. This is an excellent alcohol for us to use.
But it is obvious that there are several producers of this type of base and you can and should test the one you like best in the end.
Isopropyl Alcohol

To be quite straightforward, isopropyl alcohol is not suitable for use in perfumes, simply because it has a strong smell and is harsh on the skin. In addition, isopropyl alcohol also contains added water that will make it difficult to dilute the fragrance. In short, never use pure isopropyl alcohol for perfumery. But there is a type of perfume base that uses a small amount of it, known as a Perfumer's Formula.
Grain alcohol

Grain alcohol is simply ethanol obtained by fermenting grain. It can also be "organic" if the source material was organically grown. It doesn't matter whether the alcohol is from grain or not for perfumery; what matters is that it is cosmetic grade and undiluted (ie it must have 90% or more ethanol content).
Vodka

Yes, many recipes on the internet teach you how to make perfume using vodka. But there is a problem. Vodka is usually around 40% alcohol, which is not high enough for perfumery as you are looking for 90% or higher. In other words, don't waste your time trying to use vodka to make perfumes.
Witch Hazel Extract

I've seen recipes that use witch hazel extract as a possible substitute for alcohol in perfume making. And while the extract is a great astringent and is good for the skin, it doesn't have the level of alcohol needed to make a good perfume. In other words, it is not a real substitute for ethanol in perfumery.
Methanol

You don't have to be a chemist to know that Methanol and Ethanol are different even in name. Methanol is extremely toxic and easily absorbed through the skin. You should never consider using methanol in perfumes.

But of course if you prefer to make your own perfume base, you need more than alcohol. So in the next lecture I'll explain a perfume base recipe that you can make at home...but I remind you that perfumers alcohol, in addition to making the job easier, often have better quality materials, which will inevitably impact the the perfume you are creating.
But if you want to venture out and create your base from scratch, the next lecture will help you.
Homemade Perfume Base

You can already imagine that there are several different recipes that are used as bases for perfumes, even the ready-made bases have different compositions and that's why it's interesting to test them to see which one you prefer.
But if your intention is to create your own base, I will explain how you can do it with materials that are easy to find on the internet, since you won't always find it in the city you live in.
Basically a perfume base has 4 ingredients: alcohol, fixative, solvent and dispersant.

pages.title: Homemade base: ingredients, water and recipe

blocks.text: We've already talked about alcohol and fixatives prior to this lecture, so here I'll stick to the other two before I give you the recipe.

The solvent, in addition to helping blend the fragrance oils in the alcohol, has the function of binding the aroma molecules and slowing down their dispersion without modifying the product's formula. Together with the fixative, the solvent helps slow down the evaporation of the perfume and, consequently, gives longevity to the fragrance.

The dispersant is a very common component in cosmetics that need great absorption. Generally, in perfumery, the dispersants used are also emollients, that is, they hydrate a little so as not to leave the dry sensation that pure alcohol would leave.
Now there is a fifth ingredient that is very misunderstood in some circles: water.

So I'll start right away by saying that water can be left out. You can make your perfume base from scratch without it. I say that this subject is misunderstood because it is something that generates a lot of discussion and there are those who prefer to add water and those who prefer not to add water to their perfume. When talking about water in perfumes the questions are usually "why?", "what kind?" and "how much?" Let's start with the easy answer: "how much?"

I told you last lecture that the alcohol we use must be at least 90% Ethanol, that means it has 10% water in the composition, if the alcohol is 100% it doesn't have water at all added. If we want water, we have to add it. But how much? If you are on 100% alcohol you can add 10% or less water to the volume of alcohol. That is, in 1L of 100% ethanol you will use 10ml of water or less.

As for the question, "what kind of water?" The answer is deionized water, which is not the same as distilled water. Both distilled and deionized water are of high purity. But distilled water still contains some organic materials that have the same boiling point as water.

Deionized water is water from which all ions have been removed, the result of which chemically is a "blank slate". This water will not react with the fragrance. It won't change the odor, it won't change the color. It is the preferred water for perfumery. It's not expensive either.

Now for the question, "why use water?" It all boils down to three points: The water softens the alcohol so it feels smoother on the skin. The water clings to the top notes and gives them a persistence they wouldn't have otherwise. And, in spray, the water intensifies the effect of the perfume.

A lot of people don't like to add water because it makes the perfume cloudy, but many perfume bases already come with water added and these bases don't always get cloudy when we add the fragrance. Either way, you already know that you can test the result of your perfume base made from scratch, whether or not you add water to the mix.
But then, what about the recipe?

Here I will give you a basic recipe for 1L of perfume base using grain alcohol. Remember all the details I talked about in the last two lectures about alcohol and whether or not you need water and start testing.
• 1L of 90% or higher grain alcohol
• 10 ml of Maskanol/Dipropylene Glycol (solvent)
• 10 ml of isopropyl myristate (dispersant)
• 10 ml of fixative
If you want to add water, you can add up to 10ml, but you can try to add more if you want to test.

pages.title: Liquid perfume and reed diffuser recipes

blocks.text: Making the base is very simple: add the grain alcohol to a container, add the solvent and the dispersant. Stir the liquids well. Then add the fixative and stir again;
Liquid Perfume Recipe
After your fragrance is ready and matured, decide what type of perfume you are going to make and check the materials you will need.

Start by defining the bottle to be used so you know how much perfume you should have at the end. Let's say your chosen bottle is 100ml. So you will need about 97 ml of perfume. I always suggest leaving a space between the perfume and the bottle cap, because the spray will take up space. This leaves 2 or 3 ml of space, you can test.
Then just follow the simple steps:
1. Pour the perfume base into a beaker. Add the fragrance, stirring slowly. Be sure to stir slowly, but enough to completely disperse the fragrance in the base.
2. Now just start the process of macerating your perfume. Simple!
Reed Diffuser Recipe

Reed diffusers are very popular and today you can find these using famous perfume dupes. My students in the aromatherapy course always ask me about how to do it, but the truth is, if you want a Reed Diffuser to be as fragrant as store-bought ones or more, it's better to use good quality synthetic fragrances instead of essential oil. It will be cheaper and you will have a better result.
There are three basic components for reed diffusers:
1. The fragrance, which can even be formulated by you or a ready-made one, dupe, etc.
2. Dipropylene glycol. Which is a germicidal and also helps to dilute the essential oil or synthetic oil, helping the sticks better absorb the fragrance.
3. Perfumer's alcohol.

You will be able to test the concentrations you prefer. I find it interesting using between 30% to 40% fragrance and about 50% to 65% dipropylene glycol. A little more or a little less of any ingredient will work too, you can test it like I said. Then you add 5% to 10% perfumer's alcohol to make your formula more absorbent and easier to volatilize in the environment.
An important tip is to mix the fragrance with the dipropylene glycol and then add the perfumer's alcohol to reduce the viscosity to the desired thickness.

blocks.text: SOLID PERFUME
A Rediscovered Product

So let's talk a little more about solid perfumes. Back in the Perfume Fundamentals section I briefly talked about them and explained that it's simply a perfume with a balm-like consistency rather than a liquid.

To be honest with you, I never really paid much attention to solid perfumes until my last visit to the UK in the summer of 2022, strolling through the Brick Lane Market in London I came across this little natural cosmetics shop. In it were hundreds of beautiful cans of solid perfume.

Since then, in other markets around the city I noticed several small shops, entrepreneurs with their stalls selling either natural cosmetics or candles and there were solid perfumes. I thought it was a sign from the universe and I talked to my perfumery teacher. She referred me to a Masterclass in solid perfumes and I also did some research on the subject at the British Library.
I ended up seeing that they are really very useful to have and they are great little gifts or low cost souvenirs with all meaning and benefits.
Solid perfumes are usually made from a natural wax as a carrier for the fragrance.

And this product is not something new. It is well known and documented that since Egyptian times, aromatic balms were used in rituals, burials, and later in everyday life. We do not have documents on this, but it is possible that these balms were already used even before the Egyptian civilization.
But I said that these perfumes have some benefits, let's see them:

Less waste - Sprays can often end up going in every other direction except your skin, but a solid balm or perfume ends up directly and only where you put it. Also, solid perfume generates much less waste than regular liquid perfumes.

Portability - The small size and light weight make it ideal for carrying around when compared to a perfume bottle. You can easily slip this scent into your gym bag or even your pocket, allowing you to wear your perfume throughout the day when needed. This also makes the product much safer for flights (or shipping abroad). You know there is a restriction on the amount of liquid you can take on a flight and I've seen people literally putting bottles of perfume away to get on a flight, you're sure to have no problem keeping a solid perfume in your carry-on luggage.

Durability - A solid perfume won't break and leak its contents if you drop your bag or even the perfume itself directly on the floor. They are usually placed in a small metal can, meaning they are much stronger.

Privacy - One of the reasons this product may have done so well in Europe is its subtle nature. Sometimes, especially in a work environment, it can feel strange for a person to stop and spray themselves with perfume before starting a meeting, for example. On the other hand, it's very easy to subtly rub in some solid perfume without attracting attention. Another point is that these perfumes won't bother people close to you if you wear them. While spraying in a closed working environment can cause trouble.
Aromatherapy - For Aromatherapy lovers, this type of perfume is perfect, because it uses much less essential oil, which makes production cheaper. You can even make a therapeutic perfume

pages.title: Solid perfume recipe and method

blocks.text: using the knowledge of aromatherapy. Have you thought about it? An anti-anxiety perfume or a perfume to help with focusing?

Gentle on the skin - A liquid perfume can irritate or dry out the skin. A solid perfume will never do that as it does not contain alcohol (or even water), instead we use natural moisturizing ingredients.

Most solid perfumes usually last anywhere between 2-4 hours, meaning they don't have the lasting effect that a more expensive eau de parfum might have. However, this is partially offset by portability and ease of use, so as long as you don't mind reapplying the perfume throughout the day, this might not be a disadvantage for you.

In the Masterclass I did on these perfumes we did several tests and it became very clear that the best thing is to use beeswax because it is more stable than vegetable butter. Beeswax also lessens the chance of the perfume completely melting if accidentally left in a very hot area.

In the hands-on lecture presented here I use white flaky beeswax, which is a wax that is filtered from the impurities common to natural beeswax and does not have the strong honey aroma that beeswax commonly has. White beeswax is widely used in the cosmetics industry for its moisturizing properties, in addition to its high vitamin A content. If you prefer a vegan product, you can substitute candelilla wax for beeswax, which is 100% vegetable, but you may need to adjust the wax and oil ratio to achieve the desired texture.
Solid Perfume Recipe
This recipe makes 15g of solid perfume:
2 or 3ml - Fragrance
9g - Vegetable Butter
2g - Beeswax
5ml - Vegetable oil

Measure everything carefully and gently melt the wax and vegetable butter with the oil in a double boiler. When the wax is completely melted, remove the mixture from the heat and let it cool for a few moments, but don't let it solidify. Always observe the temperature of the mixture. Check the temperature before adding the fragrance (if you're using essential oils only add them to the mixture once it's below 60°) add the fragrance and stir well before pouring it into the container. Allow the container to cool completely before handling it.

blocks.text: POST PRODUCTION
Maturation or Macerating Fragrances, which is better?

One thing that is well known about wines is that they improve over time, they get better with aging. This process of aging wine is not a simple whim. It is important for the tannin to evolve and the wine to gain a richer and fuller flavor that our taste buds prefer.

In the world of fragrances, there are two processes that we can say are similar: maturation and maceration. Both are important in the process of creating a perfume, although some companies don't do one or the other anymore because they don't want to wait for sales to start. This results in a lower quality fragrance that even causes the overall scent of the perfume to change over time.
In my opinion, both processes are important, but there are producers who prefer just maturing or just macerating their perfume according to their tests and tastes.

You noticed that on the demonstration of creating an original fragrance, I only made a small amount. This is important because it is a test. Can you imagine me mixing a large amount of aromas and not liking the final result? I would have spent a lot of raw material and that, in addition to being expensive, is counterproductive.
So my tip is that when creating new blends, you only do it with a small amount of it at a time. Once you find a combination you like, you can blend a larger batch.

Notice that I also wrote everything down, so I was able to replicate the process here for you. I had even noted down the scents that I didn't use at the end, this is not necessary, but the ones I choose at the end and the amount of each one is very important, obviously. You will want this information later when you want to make a larger batch.

Once your perfect fragrance has been created, it's time to seal and label your amber glass bottle, place it in a cool, dark place and let it evolve and mature for 7 days. During this time, a dynamic process takes place, where the constituents of each aroma settle and interact with each other and transform into your final aroma. When it's time to revisit your creation, you can reflect on the scent, as well as take note of the things you intend to modify or change if the result at this point is not what you expected. So this is the fragrance maturation process, pretty simple, isn't it? Remember that if you are using a ready-made fragrance or a dupe you do not need to mature it, this is a necessary process only for fragrances blended by you, being it something created by you or if you're following a recipe.

Then, once you've achieved the desired fragrance result, you can do the last test continuing with the process. Then you will mix the fragrance with the other perfume ingredients, at this point you will already make use of the desired amount of fragrance according to the type of perfume you want. That is, let's say you need 10ml of fragrance to add to the perfume that will be your test subject. So you would have already prepared and matured 10ml of the fragrance you tested before, right?

Continuing, you mix the fragrance with the other ingredients of the perfume, practically finishing it and already testing it there. This will be interesting for you to get an idea of the initial aroma of the perfume once it is ready and how it will smell after maceration. As always, it's good to take notes of your impressions.

Maceration in perfumery is a period of time reserved for the ingredients to integrate in the best way, allowing the perfume to develop its entire personality and gain a high quality finish. Often without this, the perfume can have an alcohol smell, for example, although the smell of alcohol can also be due to low quality ingredients.

pages.title: Maceration methods and assessment

blocks.text: In other words, macerating the perfume is important for the product to gain quality, and is also one of the ways for the fragrance to have a better performance on the skin.
As there are several maceration techniques, each perfumery or perfumer uses a specific system or even more than one.

One of the most common is room temperature maceration. In this process, the fragrance must be kept in a container protected from light and fully sealed for 16 hours. Then, still protected from light, the perfume should be open for another 8 hours. This routine is repeated over the course of a week until the perfume is ready to use.

There is the maceration by alternating refrigeration, where the perfume undergoes a kind of thermal shock: the perfume is refrigerated in the fridge (inside a black bag) for 3 days and slowly returns to room temperature for a day. This process must be repeated 3 times, totaling 12 days, until it is ready.

The easiest maceration is done in complete darkness. In it, the perfume must be stored in a bottle or container through which no light passes on and at room temperature. In relation to the other types, this process is the simplest because we don't have to keep moving or opening the product, but it takes longer. In this case, the interesting thing is to let it macerate for at least 4 weeks.
After the maceration process you can try the perfume one more time and see how much it has changed since the first use.
If this final test is in line with what you thought, you now have the complete process of how to replicate this fragrance and create the perfume.
Assessing the Quality of your Perfume

When talking about the quality of a perfume, I think the biggest question should be: Are there aspects that are tangible or even objective, for this evaluation or is it all part of our personal preference?
In this lecture I will highlight two different perspectives to compare the quality of a perfume:
- the perspective of a perfumer
- and end-user, consumer perspectives
Obviously, there are overlaps in these views and I won't repeat them so you don't get bored.
