blocks.text: Perspective of a perfumer
When a perfumer evaluates a perfume during product development or when reviewing products on the market, they typically look at the following criteria:
1. Quality
This is the most important but also the most subjective of all the criteria here. Essentially, the question is:
Do you like the perfume?
How do you feel when using it?
But also, we look at the quality of the ingredients and the aroma:
How pure is the scent on the perfume?
How well do the scents blend together?
How complex is the final aromatic note on the perfume? If it's a singular note, how well does that work?
How does the fragrance evolve over time? How well does this change work?
Some fragrances stand out because they don't change over time. So the opposite question also applies, how well does the fragrance stay the same as the scent dries and fades?
As fragrance quality is subjective, you may decide that these are secondary issues in your assessment.
2. Originality

Is this fragrance something unusual or a fragrance that is already familiar to you the first time you try it? Does it smell like one of the countless new fragrances released every year that imitate each other?
Is it surprising?
That said, it's no use being original if it's not pleasant. It's no use wearing a fragrance if it doesn't make you feel special.
3. Power and brightness
How strong is the fragrance? Does it have the strength to project itself?
It doesn't matter how great a fragrance is, if no one can smell it, and that includes the wearer, then why are we using it?
The French use a term to describe the potency of a scent called "sillage". Another term you might find in the context of a scent's strength is 'projection'.

Silage and projection are easily confused, but they are not the same thing. Projection refers to the depth or distance to which a perfume radiates, while sillage is the trail a fragrance leaves behind.

Both describe in their own way if a perfume can make someone look for where that aroma comes from (sillage) or if it has presence (projection). Both diminish over time as they depend on the longevity of a perfume.

Then there is the question of whether a scent is perceived as strong by everyone. It may come as a surprise to you, but some people are anosmic to certain ingredients, musk being the most common example.
There are people who literally cannot smell the musky ingredients in a chord or barely notice them, and consequently feel strongly that a fragrance is weak.

Some people also have a more sensitive sense of smell than others. This affects your personal perception of a scent, even if it is of the highest quality and has excellent intensity, projection or sillage.
4. Longevity / Drying
This is the easy evaluation criteria: how long does the perfume really last on your skin?

Part of it has to do with the concentration on the perfume. And then you just have to analyze it according to the type of perfume you made and compare it with the average time of this fragrance on the body, we talk about it in the lecture that explains the types of perfumes.

The other part has to do with skin chemistry: generally speaking, perfume lasts longer on oily skin compared to dry skin, but skin flora is unique to each person and this affects how long the perfume lasts on the skin.

There is also the question of the place of application. Where you apply the perfume has an impact on longevity, regardless of its quality. What is recommended is the following: the wrists, behind the earlobes, the base of the neck, the hair, the chest and behind the knees. The more an area is covered, the longer the scent will last.
5. Versatility
At what times or by which people the fragrance can be used:
Spring, summer, fall or winter?
Everyday or special occasions?
Morning or afternoon?
In a casual or formal space?
Is it a male, female or genderless perfume?
Is it something more avant-garde or classic?

It's practically impossible to find a fragrance that fits every moment. Just like your clothes, you don't have a single item in your wardrobe that works for every occasion or every time. That's why we include this as a criterion when evaluating the quality of a perfume.
End-user/consumer assessment

When we talk about consumer evaluation, we're actually talking about the "Evaluation Criteria for a Fragrance Passionate" because few people bother to thoroughly review a perfume. Many of the criteria I've already listed that are 'perfumer' issues can also be used by a 'consumer' when evaluating fragrances. So, as I said, I won't repeat them focusing on the ones that are most exclusive to the end user:
6. Bottle and cap

It's pretty obvious, but we must like the bottle and cap of the perfume we're buying. It's going to be with us for a while and it would be very disappointing if we hated the way it looks. It's the same with a work of art: what's the point of buying something if we don't like the way it looks, even though everyone else says it's amazing.
7. Packaging and Branding

We often buy perfumes as gifts or as a gift to ourselves. 'Brands' reflect our tastes and preferences, which is why we should feel comfortable carrying a specific brand in our bag or giving it as a gift.
The way the product presents itself should be a reflection of the reason for our gift, such as the gratitude we want to express or the esteem we have for the person.
It's not just the box itself that must be beautiful, but adjacent elements like a pretty bag, delicately scented tissue paper and a pretty ribbon complete the presentation to perfection.

pages.title: Assessment: price and compliments

blocks.text: 8. Price
A general rule of thumb in the perfumery world is that the more expensive a fragrance, the better it is.

There are, however, exceptions to all the rules. Sometimes fragrance ingredients don't cost much, but they smell fantastic. Citrus is a good example. They are among the cheapest ingredients, but they bring wonderful freshness and vigor to the product.

However, the true value of a fragrance is in the 'nose' of the person who smells it. If we don't like a perfume, we are more likely to say that it is "too expensive". When we fall in love with a new perfume, on the other hand, price is rarely taken into consideration and we would rate it at least as "fair value".
9. Compliments
We also use fragrances for the benefit of those around us, just as our wardrobe.

So it would be very disappointing if we didn't get any compliments when wearing that perfume. Particularly the most artisanal fragrances will react with your skin and create an olfactory profile that is uniquely yours. A perfume from a famous brand is usually designed to ensure that the fragrance smells the same on everyone (which is not necessarily a bad thing).
Consequently, you may find that both generate praise, but for different reasons:

Famous designer brands release fragrances that are rarely polarizing, which is why few people don't like them, but it's also less likely that someone will praise you for something they smell everywhere.

Artisan perfumes offer unusual scents that can polarize opinions, but which in turn will become absolutely unique when they react with your skin flora to transform into 'you'. These fragrances are more likely to lead to the highest praise:
"You smell wonderful. What are you wearing?"

In the end, a perfume remains an emotional purchase! Therefore, it will always be difficult to rationalize a perfume perfectly, but these criteria listed in this class can be used when trying to formally evaluate a fragrance.
My advice is: Use them as mere pointers to show you a direction.

notes: Price, compliments and skin response are presented as the instructor’s subjective evaluation criteria, not reliable measures of product quality.

blocks.text: Modifications and Tests

Each time a perfumer creates a new perfume, after maceration, they test the result on the skin and on paper strips. After that an analysis is done and the ingredients in the formula can be adjusted, with things added or removed. We call this first perfume a MOD, an abbreviation for model. Evaluating each mod can require multiple uses, and a perfumer may need a few days away from the perfume to refresh their sense of smell. Working on two or more fragrances at the same time can really help too.

Of course, the ideal is for the fragrance to be completely defined when we are in the stage of making and maturing it. But the final result is only palpable when the perfume is ready. It can also happen that we think of a fragrance for an eau de parfum and it smells better as an eau de toilette. That's why tests and mods are important.

The process continues with the creation of successive mods followed by skin and paper testing, often comparing the mods against each other to determine which is the best. At some point, the perfumer asks other people to test mods. In the case of large fragrance houses, this step likely includes professional fragrance reviewers, clients and/or creative directors. Testing the formula on multiple people is important because each person's nose, skin, and preferences are different. Feedback can sometimes be contradictory; for example, some people may say the perfume has too much of one note, while others may say they prefer more of that note. The perfumer collects all the information and then tries to adjust the formula to work for as many people as possible, while fulfilling the overall fragrance concept.

Great perfumers say that creating luxury fragrances requires a few hundred modifications. It is interesting, and perhaps a little reassuring to amateur perfumers and artisans, that even grandmasters create many test mods.

As with any creative process, it can be difficult to decide when the product is ready. The perfumer by nature feels the urge to keep stirring, but eventually the formula is difficult to improve further.

Once the final mod is chosen, it's time to scale the formula for production size. Time to calculate the quantities of everything for the desired number of bottles and start the whole process of mixing aromas, maturation, then mixing with the base, maceration and only then will the perfume be ready for use and sales.
CONCLUSION
Guide to Photographing Your Creations

If you plan on selling your creations, it is necessary to stimulate the consumer's senses. And, as most marketing pieces today use visuals, I thought it was a good idea to add a lecture giving you ideas on how you can take beautiful photos of your products. Even because in the beginning the entrepreneur usually does everything alone, in the future you will have a team for that.

I like to take travel photos, but I wouldn't call myself an expert in photography, so I sat down with a friend that is a designer and photographer who helped me a lot to list everything I talk about here.

If you're going to use your smartphone for these photos, I recommend learning about all the possibilities that your device's camera gives you. There are tutorials and descriptions on youtube that can help a lot. But if you're going to use a semi-pro or professional camera, the best way to take perfume photos is with a macro lens.

This will give you the ability to focus on the label and the bottle itself. It also lets you get closer than most lenses, making it easy to capture details like the texture on the label or even the view inside the bottle itself.

The first step is to find inspiration to help you photograph better. I like to do this with travel photos and you can study some perfume photography examples too to understand more about which ideas look best and you can use the ideas to apply to your own photographs.

A tip is to search both on google and on apps such as Instagram and Pinterest. I even find Pinterest more interesting in this sense. This helps train our eyesight to see possibilities in commonplaces and with simple materials. And you don't have to copy what you see in these places, just use it as inspiration.

Then you need to choose an appropriate background that suits your subject, and by subject I mean the product you are going to photograph. Sometimes it's okay to choose a white background, it will make your perfume bottles more attractive and professional. It will also help you focus on the bottle itself rather than the background. However, you can still choose something interesting or colorful.

Here your creativity is the limit, it can be cardboard, a wall, foliage, a piece of ceramic. The perfect background can be right there in your house. Make sure you are in a good spot and that the light is good. Also, find a place where you can focus on the product and not other objects or people.

You can also use those boxes for product photos, they usually come with several backgrounds and even give you the possibility to shoot from the front or from above. A good thing is that they also come with built-in lighting.

And speaking of lighting, natural light is ideal for taking a good perfume photo because it makes your photos more beautiful and realistic. If you don't have natural light or it's too dark, try using artificial light sources such as lamps or flashlights. You can also use candles or lamps that produce warm (more yellow) light to add warmth and depth to your photos.

The wrong lighting will make your product look drab and flat - which is not what you want. You need bright light that brings out all the colors in your product. Use multiple light sources if necessary and make sure they are positioned at different angles to get even light spread across your product.

pages.title: Photography: flash, angles, props and editing

blocks.text: Try not to use flash unless absolutely necessary! Flash tends to wash out colors and make everything look dark and gray (unless you're shooting in low light). If you must use flash, try shooting with it angled down towards the subject so that it is not illuminated directly by the flash, but diffused by shadows created by other objects around you (such as a wall behind them). But this is very difficult to do if you are using a smartphone, so I would say to invest in LED lighting, nowadays it is not expensive and it delivers a great result.

Then you need to find the right angle so that your perfumes look more attractive, for example, if you want them to look like pieces of art, try top, bottom or back shots. You can also try using angles as close-ups to create an impactful visual experience.
Once you've mastered the basics of taking beautiful photos of your perfume, it's time to get even more creative by incorporating props like flowers or other objects that go well with your bottles.

Now one last tip: when you edit your photos to use on social media or on the website, don't exaggerate with the filters! Most people use too many filters when taking pictures and end up with something that looks like a cartoon instead of something real. I personally try to use very few of the filters, but if I use them it's just to improve skin tones or to reduce the amount of shine or improve the colors a bit so they look more natural.
